per_shot.note: Segmented faceted body with cyan nodes and a spark wake reads as a creature, but it floats in an overbright flat cyan pool that kills the dark, palette is ice-cyan not MAELIS sea-green/nacre, and its own light lands on nothing.

Chunky translucent plates and glowing nodes are the best creature form in this set, but low value contrast against the bright pool washes it out and the white blade head does not clearly read as the dangerous end.
A small lavender starburst inside a block, hidden directly under the pod; reads as another ore pickup, not a creature, and its glow stays inside its own cube.
Close-up shows a pleasant faceted crystal star with a soft violet halo, but it is still a decal in a tile: no bloom spill onto neighbouring ice, no threat read, and the pod body occludes it.
Grey quill tufts in dark blocks with a faint grey halo; nearly unreadable at play size, no sea-green or nacre glow, nothing says they are alive or dangerous.
Spiky fan silhouette is legible up close, but it is desaturated grey-white, emits almost no light, and reads as a mineral inclusion rather than a pressure-polyp creature.

No identifiable creature: the only candidate is a huge dark arc band with green motes that reads as void/backdrop geometry; the frame is otherwise a good MAELIS palette of sea-green fissures and brine pool.
Still no creature to read; the dark sweeping arc looks like an unlit cave ceiling, has no glow, body or dangerous end, and cannot be judged as a threat.

top_issues.issue: The Riptide does not read as a creature at all
top_issues.why: A threat the player cannot see is not a threat; the large dark arc with green specks looks like void or backdrop, breaking both 'readable at play size' and 'glow that lands'.
top_issues.suggested_direction: Give it a body made of light: a ribbon or vortex of sea-green/nacre emissive facets and particles with a bright leading head, bloom that washes the rock it passes, and a visible current direction (streaming motes, bending chevrons) so its pull reads instantly.

top_issues.issue: Frostbloom and Polyps read as ore embedded in a tile, not creatures
top_issues.why: They share the ore-in-a-cube presentation, so the player will read them as pickups; neither shows a dangerous end, motion or a threat silhouette, and the polyps are grey and nearly invisible in the dark.
top_issues.suggested_direction: Break them out of the block grid: let the frostbloom grow out of the surface with crystal petals catching the lamp and an ice-cyan core whose light spills onto adjacent ice; make polyps sea-green/nacre emissive stalks or mouths clustered on walls with a pulsing glow and a clear barb or tendril tip that signals harm.

top_issues.issue: Creature light does not land on the surrounding rock
top_issues.why: The house style (Warden, Stillwalkers, 10-creatures) is that a creature is lit by itself in the dark; here glow is confined to its own cube or lost in a bright pool.
top_issues.suggested_direction: Attach a coloured point light (or emissive-driven light pool) to each creature so neighbouring cube faces and the floor pick up its hue and fall off into dark, as the Stillwalker does on the ice around it.

top_issues.issue: Brinewyrm habitat is overbright and off-hue
top_issues.why: The pool is a flat, near-uniform bright cyan that flattens the dark, robs the translucent body of contrast, and sits in CRYOS ice-cyan with pink ore rather than MAELIS sea-green/nacre.
top_issues.suggested_direction: Darken the brine to a deep sea-green with the creature as the brightest thing in it; add nacre iridescence to its plates and keep the pool glow concentrated near the surface so the wyrm silhouettes against it.

top_issues.why: A threat must read as a threat; the wyrm's white blade head, the polyp quills and the frostbloom star are all neutral shapes with no accent colour marking where damage comes from.
top_issues.suggested_direction: Mark each hazard end with a hotter accent (brighter emissive, sharper silhouette, a jaw or barb) that contrasts with the body glow while staying within the world's hue family.

protect: Brinewyrm's chunky faceted translucent plates with glowing cyan nodes and the bright spark wake: a good low-poly creature form
The MAELIS palette of the riptide frames (sea-green fissures, glowing brine pool, green motes) is on-direction
Frostbloom's faceted crystal star and soft violet halo as an accent motif
Darkness around the frostbloom and polyps habitats; the headlamp beam with dust still reads well
